## title: "Estuary Fish Survey - Data Rescue Mission" author: "Aqilah Ali" format: html: toc: true code-fold: true execute: echo: true warning: false message: false

# Introduction

The aim of this analysis is to rescue and combine four messy datasets from a study investigating the relationship between water quality and predatory fish assemblages along the Ross River Estuary gradient.

The workflow uses mainly **tidyverse** functions to:

1.  import and clean the fish catch data;

2.  standardise site and species names;

3.  translate common fish names into accepted scientific names;

4.  clean and summarise high-frequency water-quality data;

5.  combine fish, spatial and water-quality datasets;

6.  account for zero-catch observations;

7.  calculate summary statistics; and

8.  produce a publication-ready visualisation of fish abundance along the salinity gradient.

The original raw datasets are not modified.

# 1. Load packages

``` {r}       
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(here)

# Create the output folder if it does not already exist
dir.create(
  here::here("output"),
  showWarnings = FALSE
)
```

# 2. Import the fish catch data

The fish catch data are stored across multiple Excel worksheets. Each worksheet contains observations from a site.

`excel_sheets()` identifies all worksheets, and `map_dfr()` reads and combines them into one dataset.

``` {r}        
catch_file <- here::here(
  "data/workshop2/estuary_catch_log.xlsx"
)

sheet_names <- excel_sheets(catch_file)

fish <- map_dfr(
  sheet_names,
  ~ read_excel(
    catch_file,
    sheet = .x
  )
)

fish
```

## Clean the fish data

The site and species names contain inconsistent capitalisation, spaces and underscores. These are standardised before joining the datasets.

```  {r}       
fish <- fish |>
  mutate(
    site = str_to_lower(site),
    site = str_squish(site),
    site = str_replace_all(site, " ", "_"),

    species = str_to_lower(species),
    species = str_squish(species),
    species = str_replace_all(species, " ", "_"),

    date = as.Date(date),
    count = as.numeric(count)
  ) |>
  select(
    site,
    date,
    species,
    count
  ) |>
  arrange(
    site,
    date,
    species
  )

fish
```

Check for missing or invalid fish observations:

```{r}         
fish |>
  filter(
    is.na(site) |
    is.na(date) |
    is.na(species) |
    is.na(count)
  )
```

Remove incomplete fish observations:

``` {r}        
fish <- fish |>
  drop_na(
    site,
    date,
    species,
    count
  )
```

# 3. Import and clean the species dictionary

The species dictionary provides the accepted scientific name corresponding to each local common name.

``` {r}        
species_dictionary <- read_csv(
  here::here(
    "data/workshop2/species_dictionary.csv"
  ),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

species_dictionary
```

Standardise the common names so that they match the cleaned fish dataset.

```  {r}       
species_dictionary <- species_dictionary |>
  mutate(
    common_name = str_to_lower(common_name),
    common_name = str_squish(common_name),
    common_name = str_replace_all(common_name, " ", "_")
  ) |>
  select(
    common_name,
    scientific_name
  ) |>
  arrange(common_name)

species_dictionary
```

## Translate common names into scientific names

A `left_join()` keeps every fish observation and adds the corresponding accepted scientific name.

``` {r}        
fish <- fish |>
  left_join(
    species_dictionary,
    by = c(
      "species" = "common_name"
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(
    date,
    site,
    scientific_name
  )

fish
```

Check for fish species that did not match the dictionary:

```  {r}       
fish |>
  filter(is.na(scientific_name)) |>
  select(
    site,
    date,
    species,
    count
  )
```

# 4. Import and clean site metadata

The metadata contains the spatial coordinates and estuary zone associated with each sampling site.

```  {r}       
metadata <- read_csv(
  here::here(
    "data/workshop2/estuary_metadata.csv"
  ),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

metadata
```

Standardise the site names so they can be matched to the fish dataset.

``` {r}        
metadata <- metadata |>
  mutate(
    site_key = str_to_lower(site_name),
    site_key = str_squish(site_key),
    site_key = str_replace_all(site_key, " ", "_")
  ) |>
  select(
    site_key,
    lat,
    lon,
    zone
  ) |>
  arrange(lat)

metadata
```

The `site_key` is the common identifier used to connect the metadata with the fish observations.

# 5. Join fish observations to site metadata

Create the same site key in the fish data:

``` {r}        
fish <- fish |>
  mutate(
    site_key = site
  )
```

Join the spatial information to the fish observations:

```  {r}       
fish <- fish |>
  left_join(
    metadata,
    by = "site_key"
  ) |>
  select(
    site_key,
    date,
    species,
    scientific_name,
    count,
    lat,
    lon,
    zone
  ) |>
  arrange(
    date,
    zone,
    scientific_name
  )

fish
```

Check for fish observations that did not match a site in the metadata:

``` {r}        
fish |>
  filter(is.na(zone))
```

# 6. Import and clean the sonde data

The sonde dataset contains high-frequency water-quality observations collected at 15-minute intervals.

``` {r}        
sonde <- read_csv(
  here::here(
    "data/workshop2/estuary_sonde_data.csv"
  ),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

sonde
```

## Clean the sonde data

The site names are standardised to match the fish dataset.

The timestamp is converted from a character string into a formal date-time using `dmy_hm()`.

``` {r}        
sonde <- sonde |>
  mutate(
    site = str_to_lower(site),
    site = str_squish(site),
    site = str_replace_all(site, " ", "_"),

    timestamp = dmy_hm(timestamp),

    temperature = as.numeric(temperature),
    salinity = as.numeric(salinity),
    turbidity = as.numeric(turbidity)
  ) |>
  select(
    site,
    timestamp,
    temperature,
    salinity,
    turbidity
  ) |>
  arrange(
    site,
    timestamp
  )

sonde
```

Create a daily date variable using `floor_date()` so that the high-frequency sonde data can be matched to the daily fish observations.

```  {r}       
sonde <- sonde |>
  mutate(
    date = floor_date(
      timestamp,
      unit = "day"
    )
  )
```

# 7. Reshape and quality-control the sonde data

`pivot_longer()` places the three water-quality variables into a single `variable` column. This allows the quality-control step to be applied consistently.

```  {r}       
sonde_long <- sonde |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      temperature,
      salinity,
      turbidity
    ),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  arrange(
    site,
    timestamp,
    variable
  )

sonde_long
```

## Remove invalid sensor values

The turbidity data contain the sentinel value `-999`, which represents a missing/invalid sensor reading.

Negative salinity values are also physically invalid.

These values are converted to `NA` before calculating daily means.

```   {r}      
sonde_long <- sonde_long |>
  mutate(
    value = case_when(
      variable == "turbidity" & value < 0 ~ NA_real_,
      variable == "salinity" & value < 0 ~ NA_real_,
      variable == "temperature" & (value < 0 | value > 40) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ value
    )
  )
```

Remove invalid/missing sensor observations before calculating means:

``` {r}        
sonde_long <- sonde_long |>
  drop_na(value)
```

# 8. Calculate daily water-quality means

The fish data are recorded by day, so the 15-minute sonde observations must be summarised to one daily value for each site.

``` {r}        
sonde_daily_long <- sonde_long |>
  group_by(
    site,
    date,
    variable
  ) |>
  summarise(
    daily_mean = mean(value),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(
    date,
    site,
    variable
  )

sonde_daily_long
```

## Convert the water-quality data back to columns

`pivot_wider()` creates one row per site and date, with separate columns for temperature, salinity and turbidity.

``` {r}        
sonde_daily <- sonde_daily_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = variable,
    values_from = daily_mean
  ) |>
  arrange(
    date,
    site
  )

sonde_daily
```

Rename `site` to `site_key` so it can be joined with the fish dataset:

```{r}         
sonde_daily <- sonde_daily |>
  rename(
    site_key = site
  )
```

# 9. Create the zero-catch framework

The original catch log only contains a row when a fish was recorded.

Therefore, an absent species record needs to be interpreted as **zero fish caught**, rather than as a missing observation.

`complete()` creates every combination of:

- site;

- sampling date; and

- fish species.

The missing catch values created by this process are then replaced with zero using `coalesce()`.

First, retain only the variables required to create the fish observation grid and combine duplicate observations within the same site, date and species.

```  {r}       
fish_counts <- fish |>
  group_by(
    site_key,
    date,
    scientific_name
  ) |>
  summarise(
    count = sum(count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Create the complete site × date × species framework:

```  {r}       
fish_complete <- fish_counts |>
  complete(
    site_key,
    date,
    scientific_name = species_dictionary$scientific_name
  ) |>
  mutate(
    count = coalesce(
      count,
      0
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(
    date,
    site_key,
    scientific_name
  )

fish_complete
```

Check that zero-catch observations have been created:

```   {r}      
fish_complete |>
  filter(count == 0)
```

# 10. Build the master dataset

The completed fish dataset is now joined with the spatial metadata and daily water-quality data.

Importantly, the **completed fish dataset** is used here so that zero-catch observations are retained in the final master dataset.

```  {r}       
master <- fish_complete |>
  left_join(
    metadata,
    by = "site_key"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    sonde_daily,
    by = c(
      "site_key",
      "date"
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(
    date,
    zone,
    site_key,
    scientific_name
  )

master
```

The final master dataset contains:

- site;

- sampling date;

- scientific fish species;

- fish abundance;

- latitude and longitude;

- estuary zone;

- daily mean temperature;

- daily mean salinity; and

- daily mean turbidity.

## Check the master dataset

Check the dimensions:

``` {r}        
dim(master)
```

Check the sampling sites:

```  {r}       
master |>
  select(
    site_key,
    zone,
    lat,
    lon
  ) |>
  distinct() |>
  arrange(lat)
```

Check the fish species:

``` {r}        
master |>
  select(
    scientific_name
  ) |>
  distinct() |>
  arrange(scientific_name)
```

Check for unmatched spatial or taxonomic information:

``` {r}        
master |>
  filter(
    is.na(zone) |
    is.na(lat) |
    is.na(lon) |
    is.na(scientific_name)
  )
```

# 11. Export the master dataset

The rescued master dataset is exported as a CSV file in the project's `output` folder.

``` {r}        
write_csv(
  master,
  here::here(
    "output/estuary_master_dataset.csv"
  )
)
```

# 12. Statistical extraction

The required summary table shows the **mean ± standard error (SE)** of fish abundance and salinity for each scientific species across each estuary zone.

The standard error is calculated as:

SE=SDn

where `n` is the number of observations.

```  {r}       
summary_table <- master |>
  group_by(
    scientific_name,
    zone
  ) |>
  summarise(
    mean_abundance = mean(
      count,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    se_abundance = sd(
      count,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ) / sqrt(
      sum(!is.na(count))
    ),

    mean_salinity = mean(
      salinity,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    se_salinity = sd(
      salinity,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ) / sqrt(
      sum(!is.na(salinity))
    ),

    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(
    scientific_name,
    zone
  )

summary_table
```

The resulting table contains:

- mean fish abundance;

- standard error of fish abundance;

- mean salinity; and

- standard error of salinity

for each scientific species within each estuary zone.

# 13. Prepare the salinity visualisation

The required visualisation shows fish abundance along the salinity gradient.

The estuary zones are ordered spatially from upstream to downstream.

``` {r}         
master <- master |>
  mutate(
    zone = factor(
      zone,
      levels = c(
        "Upstream",
        "Midstream",
        "Downstream"
      )
    )
  )
```

# 14. Publication-ready visualisation

Each scientific species is shown in a separate facet.

The scientific names are italicised using `theme()`.

```  {r}       
salinity_plot <- ggplot(
  master,
  aes(
    x = salinity,
    y = count,
    colour = zone
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    size = 2,
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ scientific_name,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Fish Abundance Along the Salinity Gradient",
    x = "Daily mean salinity",
    y = "Fish abundance",
    colour = "Estuary zone"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 16
    ),
    axis.title = element_text(
      face = "bold"
    ),
    strip.text = element_text(
      face = "italic",
      size = 11
    ),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

salinity_plot
```

# 15. Save the publication-ready figure

```         
ggsave(
  here::here(
    "output/fish_abundance_salinity.png"
  ),
  salinity_plot,
  width = 10,
  height = 7,
  dpi = 300
)
```

# Conclusion

The four original datasets were combined into a reproducible master dataset containing fish abundance, taxonomic information, spatial metadata and daily water-quality measurements.

The main data-rescue steps were:

- importing all Excel worksheets with `map_dfr()`;

- standardising inconsistent site and species names;

- translating common fish names into accepted scientific names with `left_join()`;

- parsing sonde timestamps with `dmy_hm()`;

- converting invalid sensor values to `NA`;

- summarising 15-minute sonde measurements into daily means;

- reshaping data with `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`;

- creating a complete site × date × species framework with `complete()`;

- replacing omitted fish observations with zero using `coalesce()`;

- joining the fish, spatial and water-quality datasets;

- calculating mean ± standard error for fish abundance and salinity; and

- visualising fish abundance along the salinity gradient using `ggplot2` and `facet_wrap()`.

The final rescued dataset is saved as:

`output/estuary_master_dataset.csv`

The publication-ready salinity figure is saved as:

`output/fish_abundance_salinity.png`
